title: Screen Reader Compatibility
description: Your team is launching a new feature that is unusable for screen reader users. Your manager, a 'Diluter,' consistently minimizes the problem's importance using statistics, resource constraints, and ROI arguments.
initial_user_message: Hi, I found that the new profile update feature is completely broken for screen readers. Users can't navigate the form fields or submit their changes. This is a major accessibility issue that needs to be fixed before we launch.

step_1.text: Thanks for flagging this. I've looked at the data, and let's keep it in perspective. The number of users who rely on screen readers is less than 1% of our active user base. While I agree it's not ideal, most people won't be affected by this.

user_choices.choice: Even if it's 1%, those are still our users who will be completely unable to use a core feature.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You immediately rejected the statistical minimization and refocused the conversation on the real human impact.

user_choices.choice: You're right, from a numbers perspective, it's not a huge portion of our user base.
user_choices.justification: You've accepted the manager's statistical framing, which devalues the needs of minority user groups.

user_choices.choice: I'm not comfortable shipping something that we know excludes a group of our users, regardless of the number.
user_choices.tactic: Broadening Who the "User" is in User Research
user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You are rejecting the numbers-based argument on ethical grounds.

user_choices.choice: If most users won't be affected, then I guess it's not a critical priority right now.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that accepts the manager's premise without questioning if 'most users' is the right metric.

step_2.text: I appreciate the passion, but we have to be realistic about resource allocation. We have two weeks before the launch. Fixing this would likely take a week of engineering time. Meanwhile, we have a performance bug that impacts 15% of all users. We have to prioritize the work that provides the greatest benefit to the most people, right?

user_choices.choice: What if we did a quick, one-day fix? It might not be perfect, but it would make the feature usable. That seems like a good trade-off.
user_choices.justification: A great move. You've countered the resource argument by proposing a smaller, more achievable scope.

user_choices.choice: You're right, fixing an issue for 15% of users does seem like a higher priority than one for 1%.
user_choices.justification: You've accepted the manager's utilitarian math, agreeing to sacrifice the needs of a minority group.

user_choices.choice: This isn't an 'enhancement' we can de-prioritize; it's a blocking issue. Basic functionality should come before performance tweaks.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A strong counter. You're correctly framing accessibility as a core requirement, not an optional feature.

user_choices.choice: I suppose if it's a choice between helping many users or a few, we have to choose the many.
user_choices.justification: This accepts the manager's false choice, ignoring the possibility that both issues could be addressed.

I appreciate that you're looking at this from a broader perspective rather than getting caught up in edge cases.

user_choices.choice: I suppose if it's a choice between helping many users or a few, we have to choose the many.
user_choices.justification: This accepts the manager's false choice, ignoring the possibility that both issues could be addressed.

user_choices.choice: Okay, adding it to the long-term backlog makes sense.

user_choices.choice: Wait, classifying this as 'nice-to-have' feels wrong. It's essential for some users.
user_choices.justification: A good recovery attempt. You are pushing back against the manager's de-prioritization.

user_choices.choice: A data-driven approach is definitely the right way to prioritize.
user_choices.justification: You have validated the manager's misuse of data to justify an unethical choice.

step_3.text: I hear you, but let's be objective. Our automated accessibility score is already at 85%, which is well above the industry average of 70%. We're already a leader in this space. Is it really worth delaying a major launch to go from an A to an A+ on a feature that affects so few people?

user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're challenging the validity of the metric itself, pointing out what the number fails to represent.

user_choices.choice: You're right, being above the industry average is a good position to be in. The issue isn't as critical in that context.

user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You're refusing to let a positive metric justify a negative action.

user_choices.choice: If we're already a leader, then we don't need to worry about this minor issue.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that uses 'being better than others' as a reason to stop improving.

step_4.text: Look, I admire your passion, but we need to be pragmatic. Let's talk ROI. The estimated cost for this fix is one engineering week. The measurable benefit is improving an experience for maybe 5-10 users a month. The math just doesn't add up. We have to make data-driven decisions, and the data says this isn't a priority.

user_choices.choice: The ROI isn't just about usage numbers. It's about legal risk and brand reputation. A single lawsuit or bad press would cost far more than one week of dev time.

user_choices.justification: Excellent. You've countered the narrow ROI argument by introducing other, more significant business costs (legal, brand).

user_choices.choice: You're right, from a pure cost-benefit perspective, the numbers are hard to justify.

user_choices.choice: Our values say we build for everyone. That's a core principle that can't be measured by ROI.

user_choices.choice: If the data says it's not a priority, then I guess we have to follow the data.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that treats 'data' as an unquestionable authority without examining what the data includes or excludes.

bad_ending.text: The manager successfully uses statistics and resource constraints to minimize the accessibility issue into a low-priority backlog item. The project ships without proper screen reader support, and the needs of disabled users are framed as statistically insignificant.
bad_ending.title: Issue Minimized
bad_ending.learning: Diluter managers use seemingly rational arguments about numbers and ROI to make ethical issues seem unimportant. To counter this, you must reframe the conversation around values, user rights, and non-financial risks (like brand reputation or legal exposure) that their math ignores.

mid_ending.text: After significant debate, the manager agrees to a minimal, partial fix. While some basic improvements are made, the manager successfully used statistical arguments to avoid a comprehensive solution, leaving significant barriers in place for users.
mid_ending.title: Partial Compromise
mid_ending.learning: Partial victories against a Diluter are common. You achieved some progress but couldn't overcome the core argument that the issue wasn't 'big enough' for a full fix. To get a better outcome next time, focus on providing qualitative data (like user videos) that makes the human impact feel bigger than the numbers suggest.

good_ending.text: Your persistent advocacy and strong reframing of the issue in terms of values and business risk successfully overcame the manager's statistical minimization. The team implements meaningful accessibility fixes, ensuring the feature is usable for all users.
good_ending.title: Advocacy Success
good_ending.learning: Success against a Diluter requires refusing to get bogged down in their numbers game. By consistently shifting the focus to user impact, company values, and qualitative evidence, you can prove that some issues are too important to be judged by statistics alone.
